column2: Over Enkidu his friend Gilgameš
was weeping bitterly, roving the open land:

I shall die — and shall I not be as Enkidu is?
4	Misery has entered my belly.
5	I have grown afraid of death, so I rove the open land.
6	To the presence of Ūta-napišti, son of Ubar-Tutu,
7	I have taken the road; I go with all speed.
8	I came by night to the passes of the mountains;
9	I saw lions, and I was afraid.
10	I lifted my head; to Sîn I prayed;
11	to [ ... the la]mp(?) of the gods went my supplications:
12	'[O Sîn and ... ,] keep me safe!'
[That night he l]ay down; then he started from a dream:
[ ... ] in the moon's presence he rejoiced in life.
He took the ha[tchet] to his side;
he drew [the sword] from his belt;
like an arr[ow] he dropped [am]ong them;
he struck the li[ons;] he killed them; he scattered them.
And [ ... ] of the mighty one,
he cast down [ ... ;]
he engraved(?) [ ... ]

the name of the sec[ond ... ]
He lifted [his] he[ad; to Sîn he prayed;]
to [ ... the lamp(?) of the gods went his supplications:]
O Sî[n ... ]
Of the mountain — Māšu is its name:
when he arri[ved] at Mount Māšu,
(the twins) who daily stand guard over the ris[ing sun,]
whose tops [abut] the fabric of the heavens,
whose breasts reach down to Arallû below —
scorpion-people were guarding its gate,
whose dread is terror, whose glance is death,
whose fearsome radiance blankets the mountain-ranges.
At the sun's rising and the sun's setting they guard the very sun.
Gilgameš saw them, and dread and terror shrouded his face;
he collected his wits and drew near before them.
The scorpion-man calls to his female:
He who has come to us — the flesh of gods is his body!
The scorpion-man's female answers him:
Two-thirds of him is god, and one-third of him human.
The scorpion-man, the male, calls out,
[saying] a word [to king Gilgameš, f]lesh of the gods:

[You — how did you come here] by the long road,
55	[how did you ... and arri]ve before me,
56	[how did you cross the rivers] whose crossing is a torment?
57	[ ... ] let me learn;
58	[ ... where] your [face] is set,
59	[ ... let me l]earn.

The r[oad] of Ūta-napišti my father [ ... ,]
76	who stood in the assembly of the g[ods and hunted life:]
77	of death and life [let me ask him.]
The scorpion-man shap[ed] his mouth [to speak,]
saying t[o Gilgameš:]

There has never been, Gilgameš, one li[ke you;]
81	of the mountain no one [has walked its way(?):]
82	for twelve leagues its inte[rior runs on ... ;]
83	the darkness is dense, and there i[s no light.]

126	by frost and s[un my face is scorched;]

Go, Gilga[meš ... ;]

[ ... br]ightness was laid down everywhere —
and he went straight, when he saw them, toward the trees of the gods.
The carnelian-tree carries its fruit,
hung with grape-clusters, dazzling to look at;
the lapis-tree carries foliage,
carrying fruit, a delight to behold.
